newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn upbeat on economy but experts cautious.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn upbeat on economy but experts cautious.

text.p: German leaders painted an upbeat picture of the economy on Friday and said Bonn would qualify for European economic and monetary union, but economists said the government view was too rosy.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel both said Germany would cut the budget deficit enough this year to join EMU's planned start in 1999. Accelerating growth would leave a comfortable margin on the deficit next year.
"For me it is clear: Germany will fulfil the criteria. The euro will come at the agreed time," Kohl told Bonn journalists at his traditional pre-holiday news conference.
Kohl said the German economy was gaining momentum and stuck to the official view of 2-1/2 percent growth this year. He said output could rise by as much as three percent in 1998.
He also played down recent weakness in the German mark, which fell this week to six-year lows at 1.8040 to the dollar.

"When exports used to go badly because of a weak dollar, people complained," Kohl said. "Now things are going a bit the other way, which is not earth-shaking, it does not mean that we should start moaning again."

Adding to recent low-key official comments, a senior central banker said the mark at present levels would not ignite inflation because the impact of higher import prices would be curbed by high unemployment.
"The depreciation of a currency in itself always has an impact on import prices," Bundesbank council member Guntram Palm told Reuters.

"But given that the economy is by no means foaming over, given continued labour market problems and the far-reaching consequences of companies boosting productivity and cutting costs, I see no appreciable deterioration of the domestic price climate at present."

A further significant dollar rise would have to be closely monitored but the dollar exchange rate on its own did not determine the Bundesbank's monetary policy, said Palm, who is president of the state central bank of Baden-Wuerttemberg.
Waigel, who has intervened verbally in support of the mark this week, made no comment on currencies on Friday.

But, speaking in Munich, he gave assurances Bonn would hit the Maastricht treaty budget deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product this year. Germany would undershoot the ceiling in 1998 "with a sufficient margin".

Germany's efforts to contain borrowing have been hamstrung by record postwar unemployment -- a drain on tax revenues which has also swelled social security costs. But Waigel said better growth prospects next year would help erode unemployment now at over four million.
Economists were less positive after the latest Ifo research institute index of business confidence rose in June to 96.0 from 95.4 in May, while business expectations index fell back.

"The economic recovery is progressing further, but in a very moderate way," Ifo president Karl-Heinrich Oppenlaender said in Munich. He said the fall in business expectations reflected growing uncertainty among companies and investors.
Ruediger Pohl, head of the IWH economic research institute, was also less sanguine than Kohl and Waigel on both the budget deficit and the economy.
"Based on the current trends, I find 3.0 percent hard to imagine," Pohl told Reuters in the east German town of Halle.
Pohl said, however, that a deficit of 3.4 percent of GDP this year should be no obstacle to Germany joining EMU at its planned start in 1999.

In its latest economic forecast, the IWH also predicted economic growth of just two percent this year, rising to 2.5 percent in 1998. Unemployment will remain stubbornly high at a rate of 11.3 percent both this year and next, it forecast.

Both Kohl and Waigel were reluctant to comment on France's chances of qualifying for EMU after admissions by Paris that its budget deficit would overshoot the strict Maastricht goal this year. An independent audit next week is expected to show that the French deficit will hit 3.5 percent of GDP this year.
"We should leave the French to do what they themselves want to do. It is not for me to say," Kohl said in answer to a question on France's EMU prospects.

But there was dissent from one EMU hardliner in Waigel's own Bavarian-based Christian Social Union (CSU) party. Michael Glos, who leads the CSU's parliamentary group, said postponing EMU should be considered if France flunks the criteria.

"France is the key to the common euro, since a precondition for starting is that we and France are on board. If France misses the goals then we must talk about a delay," Glos told the Passauer Neue Presse in an interview to run on Saturday.
-- douglas.busvine@reuters.bon (Bonn 49-228-26097150)
